questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Please explain: *
Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: A mix of cultural differences and good academic institutions, particularly for computer science. I wanted to learn more about AI while experiencing a place that had its own very distinct character and to be culture shocked in a good way. Another good thing is that young Koreans are decent at English while Korea remains culturally very Korean.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I am super happy with my courses, and their program SNU buddy which was great socially. Downsides were the amount of paper work to navigate particularly around on campus accommodation that required some medical documentation.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: There was a lot of paperwork, regarding ARC visa and accomodation as well as course selection. Most of it was before arrival but generally you receive a lot of infomration, and long instructions. So you can find a lot of information but navigating it takes some time.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: They have a good center for foreign students with people you can mail. They are used to handling foreign students and have a lot of foreign students at the school. You can get help if you need it.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: While they are super helpful they can also be quite rigid in their systems which can be quite complex or specific.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: They have a large amount of on campus housing Gwanak residence dorms. It is shared accomodation so you share a room with someone. It is very cheap around 1500 dkk per month, however to get the right stamps and medical record you can expect to pay 1000 to 2000 dkk or more before knowing if you have any chanse of getting a place. They use a randomized queue system. I first moved to a Goshiwon near SNU station, the first month and was offered a room the second month. Goshiwon is great for flexible student housing but it can be very small. I lived at "All is well home", clean but super small. My general perception is that although VISA will require lots of paperwork goshiwon will provide it and may be used to it at least mine did. Korea generally feels very safe and I never felt like I was beeing scammed or so regarding housing.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: People generally don't cook much here, they eat convenient store food, or eat out most the time. On campus there are great cafeteria options that I used most of the time. Both in goshiwon or the dorms there are shared cooking facilities if you want to cook. Cafeteria meals typically go for 1000-7000 KRW (they have one budget option for 1000 krw), and a cheap meal out goes for 7000 - 20000 krw.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer:
1. The medical documentation can be tricky to get, you have to have the right stamps on the right form. You need to fetch NPR measles vaccine data from when you were a kid. Also I did chest xray and vaccine proof separately, they asked me to transfer it to the same page, which would cost 1500 dkk just to sign. I just ended up sending what i had and they reluctantly accepted once there. You are not guaranteed housing if you send this in, it is just for you to participate in the lottery.

2. It is easier to find temporary / student accommodation through goshiwons around SNU station than it would be in Denmark. Generally I still recommend on campus, since you get convenient access to cafeteria, library, at night. But if you care less about studies, and more about going to new palces living off campus near the station might be better faster access to the city.

3. It is humid and it might be a bit moldy. You don't know what room you will get before hand. It was not super clean when i moved in but we cleaned up and I came to terms with it. Overall I think its fine, youre not there forever.

4. Privacy, you will most likely share a room. Also when signing up I recommend singing up for all types of housing including the shared dorms if you want a good chanse of getting in. Generally the Koreans are very polite and sharing was not a problem for me.

What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *

Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
Generally their systems are difficult. I first applied to CSE, the computer science department. This is very difficult to get into however. I was rejected. I then applied to Departement of Liberal Studies and got in, this is much easier. For tecnically you can apply to courses across departments, but for undergrad a lot of them are restricted to only students at their departement, keep in mind you are only selected amongst English courses with is a subset in the first place. My solution was to only take grad courses, they have less restrictions and more English courses. SNU recommends 5 undergrad courses for one semester or 3 grad so keep in mind that the conversion to ECTS may depend on this. I think i used 1 grad course to 10 ECTS and one undergrad course to 6 ECTS, but you will have to check this individually with KU.

The course registration itself is a multi stage process. It has several "first come first served" type steps, for which you need to be awake in the middle of the night, clicking a button in their system as fast as you can. I recommend checking their system server time using time.navyism. If you dont get your desired courses the first time there is a decent chanse to change once you are there as well, through a course change period when other people change courses spots open up and you can apply.

I ended up getting a great schedule but there is lots of uncertainty in the process and lots of planning. You should go into it knowing you may not get to study what you want, but you will most likely get some of what you want.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: You can email them, they send out lots of info and long pdfs as well.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got a great schedule but there was no guarantees for it.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Be open minded in terms of what courses you get, and really try to switch if you are unhappy once you get there, there is a decent chance a spot opens up.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Courses were generally good. They are generally broader and more surface level than KU, you generally dont have lots of past tests to practise on. Grad courses are generally more reserach oriented, you may present papers etc. The style of education and difficulty depends a lot on the proffessor.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I had: Deep Learning, Advanced Deep Learning, Topics in Micro Economics, Topics in Operations Management. Some courses were academically very difficult, but the expectation in terms of evaluation were not that difficult to meet.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: No past tests to practise on, no exercise classes with TA like DIKU, some homework. Generally more surface level but more different topics. More paper presentations and academic discussions. But then also keep in mind i am BA at DIKU and did MA courses at SNU

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: Deep Learning, Advanced Deep Learning, Topics In Micro Economics, Topics In Operations Management

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your second semester. *
What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Deep Learning, is great to get overview of all kinds of deep learning methods. I heard RL is too easy and I also took Adv Deep Learning, its mostly paper presentations and a project. Its great if you want to try something applied in AI but it feels PHD level. Topics In operations management is great MBA style teaching not too difficult teacher is great. Topics in Micro was way too mathematical, also feels PHD level, class was almost empty, don't recommend unless you're really interested in the mathematics of game theory. It is not taught very pedagogically.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Eating out is cheap, student housing is cheap, flight was cheaper than expected.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: SNU buddy is great, its really well executed and provides activities most weeks, plus a pub. Great way to get to know people.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There is a lot, I joined swimming but only had time to go two times because its on a Saturday and you want to do other things then. But they show a lot of clubs in the semester start at the front lawn near building 63.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Swimming, tennis, SNU buddy, go out to Ittaewon, dinners Korean BBQ etc, see other Korean cities.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Travel around Asia, I went to Japan twice, wish I had time to see China and Taiwan as well.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Young people generally speak english which helps a lot. Everything is different but you learn fast.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: SNU buddy

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Not sure, they are super polite and also quite social.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: That there is a different way of doing everything we do here that also works. Good perspective. Love the food and that locals are out eating and enjoying the city also super safe.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: Join SNU buddy, remember its pass fail, so take cool/difficult courses if you want, also might be smart to take some easier course so you have time to see things and enjoy. See Japan as well.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: No

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Getting to know new people through classes and exchange program.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Paper work ARC visa, phone number, bank card, medical documentation, course registration.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: What I did: Flight, etihad airways, quite cheap, free hotel stopover in Abudabi on my way back, book home trip separate as you may find out you want to travel more. Phone nr, bought on campus sim card in building 63. Bank Shinhan on campus you can open account before ARC and set up auto transfer as required by student housing, then get card once you get ARC. Otherwise Hire visa (you apply for ARC with them) also had an option to get bank account while application was pending. Get a good photo, with white background that works with ARC demands so you can use it not only for visa but for ARC. Transportation, buy t-money at airport in vending machine. If you have a period when you want to travel a lot, buy climate card for a month or a a week which is unlimited travel in Seoul. If you dont get campus housing, start with a cheap goshiwon near SNU station and figure it out as you go. If you have money to spend there are also great share houses in that area I know friends that loved that.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
